detect-names-and-quotes-no-score:
Very strongly. Nearly every phrase is a default choice, and the two sentences hold no concrete fact.

- "isn't just a tool - it's a partner": the not-X-but-Y move. It knocks down a claim nobody made so the second half sounds bigger, and the spaced hyphen is standing in for an em dash.
- "stands as a testament to": inflated significance, and a way of avoiding a plain "is" or "shows".
- "In today's fast-paced digital landscape": a stock throat-clearing opener. "Landscape" used figuratively is standard model vocabulary.
- "pivotal commitment", "seamless", "vibrant collaboration": model vocabulary stacked three deep in one sentence. "Pivotal commitment" is also an odd pairing, since a commitment isn't the kind of thing that pivots anything.
- "empowering teams to unlock their full potential": an -ing phrase tacked onto the end to sound like analysis, with no claim anyone could check.
- The passage as a whole: it would read the same pasted into any other company's website. It never says what the platform does, who uses it, or what changes for them.

Nothing here reads as a particular person: no specific detail, no odd word choice, no product name doing real work. Selling is fine in marketing copy. What gives this away is that it sells in general terms instead of pointing to something concrete. All of this shows default phrasing, not who typed it.

Dear Orla,

My name is Dan and I run ScentVerdict, a fragrance review site I started last year after getting frustrated with how hard it was to find honest reviews of niche perfumes.

We go into every fragrance we cover in depth. Each review is based on at least two weeks of wear, and we score longevity, projection and value separately, because a single star rating hides too much. Over the last twelve months we have published 2,400 reviews, and our readers tell us the separate scores are the reason they come back.

I have been following your house for a while, and I think your approach to small-batch releases is exactly the kind of story our readers care about. I would love to review your autumn collection. I would also be happy to share our methodology in more detail, including how we handle samples, how we disclose free products and how we make sure the review is independent of any commercial relationship.

We also run a monthly newsletter that goes to our most engaged readers, and we have a small but growing presence on Instagram and TikTok, where short wear-test videos have done particularly well.

If this sounds interesting, please do get in touch. I would be delighted to set up a call at a time that suits you.

Kind regards,
Dan

Overshare (not cut):
- "Small but growing" tells a founder you are pitching that your social reach is thin, before she has asked about it.
First contact (not cut): 220 words. Paragraph 2 and paragraph 4 are detail a link to your site or methodology page could carry.
